stories.headline: Update: Iranian Missile and Drone Attack Starts Fire at Industrial Facility in Bahrain
stories.summary:
Bahrain said an Iranian attack struck a civilian industrial facility late Saturday, starting a fire in the latest escalation of the war in the Middle East. The Bahrain Defence Force said its air defences intercepted a number of Iranian aerial attacks. The Interior Ministry described the strike as part of "Iranian aggression," said preliminary reports pointed to material damage but no injuries, and said civil defence teams were working to contain the blaze. It did not name the facility or its location. Earlier, air raid sirens sounded and residents were urged to move to the nearest safe place.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it carried out a combined missile and drone operation against US military positions at the al-Riffa and Awali bases in Bahrain. It claimed to have destroyed two US Patriot air defence radars. The IRGC said the action responded to "continued aggression and violations of the airspace of the Islamic Republic of Iran," citing two US MQ-1 and MQ-9 drones it said had entered Iranian airspace. Iranian outlets gave conflicting accounts: Fars reported attacks on bases at Sheikh Isa and Juffair, while IRNA reported that an interceptor missile launched from the US Fifth Fleet base crashed on Sitra Island and started a large fire, blaming a Patriot system malfunction.

Bahrain hosts the US Navy's Fifth Fleet and has been attacked repeatedly since the war began, including three drone attacks in recent days after a lull of several weeks. Gulf Arab states have come under repeated fire from Tehran since the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28. The renewed strikes come as Washington debates its next steps in the conflict, and the Senate recently rejected an Iran war powers resolution 48-51. Claims from both sides have not been independently verified.

stories.headline: Congress Recesses With Several House Races Still Uncalled Nearly Three Weeks After Midterms
stories.summary:
Lawmakers left Capitol Hill on Saturday after a week of moving bills and confirming appointments, as the 119th Congress works to complete its legislative priorities before it adjourns for good in January. Speaker Mike Johnson and other leaders in both parties voiced frustration this week over members' low attendance. Several House races remain uncalled nearly three weeks after the election, even as Democrats have claimed majorities in both chambers.

The transition is shaping policy fights. Democrats have finalized sweeping midterm wins, and Republicans are weighing the causes of their losses. Vice President JD Vance blamed the defeats on voter anger over the Iran war and oil prices, while declining to endorse President Trump's claim that Iran was close to a nuclear weapon in February. Trump has said he would launch the war again. Trump also said bipartisanship with House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries could produce "tremendous things," citing healthcare and a 10 percent credit card rate cap.

The week also brought moves on Senate confirmations. Sen. Thom Tillis, a retiring North Carolina Republican, reportedly blocked a vote on Michael LoSapio, Trump's nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, after LoSapio said at his hearing that he did not believe January 6, 2021 was an attack. The White House also fired National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross amid a wave of tech outages, and the FDA nominee withdrawal left that agency without a confirmed leader. Congress returns with limited time before Democrats take control, and several undecided House seats could affect the margin.

stories.headline: Update: Brazil's Jair Bolsonaro Admitted to Intensive Care With Intestinal Obstruction
stories.summary:
Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro was admitted to an intensive care unit with an acute intestinal obstruction on Saturday, according to a statement from the hospital. He had earlier been hospitalized with severe abdominal pain. The hospital said he is stable and breathing on his own.

Bolsonaro is serving a sentence for plotting a coup, which makes his health a matter of national political significance in Brazil. Any decision on his custody, including requests to move him to house arrest on medical grounds, would fall to the courts.

The hospital did not immediately say how long he would remain in intensive care or whether surgery was planned. Further medical updates are expected in the coming days.

stories.headline: Cost-of-Living Protests Sweep Across European Cities
stories.summary:
Protests took place across European cities on Friday as marches were held over the cost of living and other grievances, including housing shortages and underfunding in education. Demonstrations were reported in Germany, France, Croatia, Italy and the United Kingdom, among other countries, and drew many young adults.

In Rome, thousands of people took part in a march organised by Italy's main trade union, according to the BBC's Europe correspondent Nick Beake, who reported from the scene.

The breadth of the demonstrations points to economic pressure on households across the continent. Organizers cited affordability of housing and public services as central concerns, and it remains to be seen whether governments will respond with policy changes.

stories.headline: Trump Signs Order Limiting Congress's Access to Contractor and Agency Information Ahead of Democratic Takeover
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order late Friday titled "Protecting the Executive's Privileges and Enhancing Efficiencies in Federal Contracting." It directs federal contractors and subcontractors to notify the White House of any congressional requests for their communications. It also directs them to withhold material the administration considers privileged. The order is widely seen as a response to expected aggressive oversight from Democrats, who won majorities in both chambers in the midterm elections and take control in January.

Under the order, companies must coordinate with the White House and federal agencies on "appropriate responses" to congressional inquiries. The White House warned that contractors who fail to comply could have their contracts terminated and their future federal work suspended. The order asserts that Congress's ability to seek confidential information about the executive branch is limited.

Supporters, including right-leaning outlets, framed the order as a move to fortify the presidency against what they described as the weaponization of oversight by a Democratic-controlled Congress. Critics, including Democrats and left-leaning outlets, described it as an effort to stymie legitimate investigations into the administration and its associates. Incoming Democratic leaders have signaled wide-ranging probes.

The order was signed as Congress left Washington for a recess after a week of confirmations and bills. Legal challenges and fights over contractor compliance are likely once the new Congress is seated.

stories.headline: Russia-Bound Cargo Ship Hit by Drone Attack in Gulf of Finland
stories.summary:
A Russian cargo vessel bound for the Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland on Saturday morning, Russian and Finnish authorities said. The ship, the Sparta II, caught fire and drifted into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack, and Kyiv has not commented.

Finland's coast guard said it was alerted at about 08:50 local time, and the vessel was located roughly 50 km west of Suursaari island. Kaliningrad's governor said two drones were used and that there was no threat to the territory's supplies. The crew was evacuated to another Russian vessel, and Finnish officials reported no environmental damage or danger to maritime traffic. Finland also said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating its airspace, possibly during rescue or tracking operations.

Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said "war is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," adding that "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor." The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and by Ukraine this year, and its operator was established within Russia's defence ministry structure. Finland's Border Guard is leading the investigation, and NATO has been informed.

The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the war, with Ukraine expanding long-range strikes beyond the front lines. Earlier this month a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.

stories.headline: Update: Virginia Reports First Measles Death of 2026 as U.S. Outbreak Nears 6,000 Cases
stories.summary:
Virginia's health department said Friday that a child aged four or younger died after testing positive for measles. It is the state's first measles-related death this year. Officials declined to share further details, including the child's vaccination status, citing the family's privacy.

The death comes amid the largest U.S. measles outbreak in decades. Data tracked from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention indicate more than 5,800 confirmed cases nationwide in 2026, the highest total since 1991, with cases reported in 47 of the 52 jurisdictions in the agency's registry. States have reported 10 deaths this year. The outbreak recently cost the United States its measles elimination status, which it had held for 26 years.

The CDC updates its case counts weekly, and public health officials have continued to stress that measles spreads easily among unvaccinated people and can be especially dangerous to young children. The Virginia death adds to the pressure on state and federal health agencies as the case count approaches 6,000.

stories.headline: Cotton Says Lutnick Ignored 'Many Letters' Warning About AI Chip Sales to China
stories.summary:
Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., said Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick repeatedly ignored his warnings that advanced U.S. AI chips were being smuggled into China. His remarks came after reports surfaced about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Cotton said that if Lutnick wanted his support, he should have responded to his many letters on the subject. The criticism from a senior Republican on national security matters is notable because it targets a Cabinet member in the Trump administration.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent addressed the issue in an interview with CNBC after returning from a trip to Asia with President Trump. He said the proper chip restrictions are in place and that remote access to the chips has been curtailed. California officials have separately subpoenaed Nvidia over whether China improperly obtained chips or information.

The dispute adds to scrutiny of export controls on AI hardware at a time when markets are anxious about the technology sector. It is not yet clear whether Lutnick will respond publicly or whether Congress will press for hearings.

stories.headline: Update: UK and EU Deal Will Take Effect Regardless of Tuition Fees Talks, Miliband Says
stories.summary:
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told the BBC that the agreement reached Friday between the UK and the European Union will come into force whether or not the two sides negotiate a separate tuition fees deal. The package includes scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, along with a new youth mobility scheme.

A proposal to lower tuition fees for EU students in the UK was not agreed. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was confident a solution would be found, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham added "me too." EU sources had earlier suggested the bloc might hold up the wider deal until the fees question was settled, but Miliband said it was absolutely clear the agreements would apply and that legislation would be introduced in Parliament.

Burnham called the deal a win-win that could lower the cost of living and reduce red tape, and said the Treasury believes it could boost the economy by up to 17 billion pounds a year. Miliband said there would be no cost to taxpayers and no new contributions to the EU budget.

Asked whether rejoining the EU would be considered, Miliband said all options would be on the table. Burnham said he would discuss ideas for even closer ties in coming months.

stories.headline: Update: Texas Defends Execution of Reinaldo Dennes as Witness Describes 'Tremendous Distress'
stories.summary:
A Texas official on Friday defended the state's execution of Reinaldo Dennes, 70, who loudly said he was in pain during a lethal injection that followed a struggle to find a suitable vein. Texas Department of Criminal Justice spokesperson Amanda Hernandez said all processes and procedures were followed and that it was carried out as planned.

According to the department, Dennes was strapped to the gurney at 6:04 p.m. and an IV was placed in his neck at 6:20 p.m., with a second line in his foot at 6:38 p.m. Drugs began flowing less than a minute after his final statement began at 6:52 p.m. Dennes exclaimed, "The pain! Go! Go!" and said, "Don't let me suffer like this." He was declared dead at 7:08 p.m.

His spiritual adviser, the Rev. Jeff Hood, a death penalty opponent, said he felt as if he were holding a bucking bronco and called the execution torture. Hernandez said there is no normal time limit and that the aim is to do it correctly, and she did not know how many attempts were made to place IV lines.

It was Texas' ninth execution this year. Scrutiny of lethal injection has grown since Christa Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital in Tennessee in September, and Tennessee called off another execution in May after failing to establish an IV line.

stories.headline: Anthropic Mathematician Claims Claude Helped Prove Riemann Hypothesis
stories.summary:
Levent Alpoge, a mathematician employed by Anthropic, said Friday that he used a non-public version of the company's Claude AI model to produce a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics. He said the work took about six weeks. The claim came a day after Anthropic's U.S. stock market debut.

The hypothesis, nearly 170 years old, concerns the distribution of prime numbers, which underpin much of higher mathematics and cryptography. If correct, the proof would rank among the most significant in history. The complete proof, written in the Lean computer language used to verify proofs, runs over 250,000 pages.

Alpoge acknowledged that the timing is awkward, writing that it is "horrible" but that the cynical view tied to the listing is "false." Prominent mathematician Terence Tao said verification is still some way off and that the digestion process will take time, though a human author is available to help. OpenAI claimed in September that its tools solved part of the Navier-Stokes problem, a result not yet confirmed and criticized by some academics, and groups of scholars have warned about AI firms boasting of major solutions.

stories.headline: Mexican Army Captures FBI Ten Most Wanted Fugitive 'Chapo Isidro' in Sinaloa
stories.summary:
Mexico's military captured Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro," in Guasave, in Sinaloa state, after a gun battle erupted during the operation. He was on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted list. Mexican authorities allege he leads a cartel responsible for drug distribution and importation.

The arrest is being described as a significant victory for the Mexican government, which has faced pressure from Washington over cartel violence and fentanyl trafficking. Details on injuries or casualties from the gunfire were not immediately available in the reporting.

It remains to be seen whether Meza-Flores will be extradited to the United States, where he faces charges that placed him on the FBI list. Trump designated illicit fentanyl a weapon of mass destruction nearly a year ago, and the capture adds to a continuing U.S.-Mexico effort against trafficking organizations.

stories.headline: Fed Officials Warn AI Boom Is Adding to Inflation Risks Ahead of Expected December Rate Hike
stories.summary:
A growing number of Federal Reserve officials are warning that the artificial intelligence buildout is adding to inflation pressures. Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said Monday that the AI build-out is "exerting upward pressure on demand and inflation," though future productivity gains could eventually ease prices. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Thursday that nearly unprecedented business investment risks overheating, likening it to a "pig through the python."

Minutes from the Fed's October meeting showed many officials view the buildout as a material source of inflation risk. Producer prices for electrical components are up nearly 32% from a year ago, and electrical machinery is up 14.3%, with consumer electronics also rising. Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, and economists estimate roughly 4% annual inflation.

The Fed is also contending with an energy shock from the Iran war and lingering effects of tariffs, with inflation above target for more than five years. Investors and economists widely expect a rate increase at the December meeting. Officials have also raised concerns about financial system risks if the AI buildout goes bust, a worry that echoes Friday's market correction.

stories.headline: Update: FBI Investigating Apparent Breach of Its National Crime Information Database
stories.summary:
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of the National Crime Information Center, the nationwide database federal, state and local law enforcement use to share information on warrants and background checks. Two people briefed on the matter told NBC News and other outlets about the breach. CNN reported it first on Friday evening. The FBI had no comment as of Friday night.

NBC also reported an apparent cyberattack on the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Employees were told Thursday that the system used to pay farmers had been targeted. USDA officials said no other systems had been hit as of Friday, but they warned that the hackers could find a way into more sensitive information. The department has not commented publicly.

The reports follow a week of tech outages that disrupted banking, air traffic control and other sectors. Officials have said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks, but they have drawn scrutiny from lawmakers. White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with President Trump saying he was not good enough.

The FBI has been targeted before. In September, the bureau said it was investigating an apparent breach by the cybercrime group ShinyHunters, which claimed to have stolen sensitive information on all of the bureau's roughly 38,000 employees. The scope of the NCIC intrusion and who is responsible remain unclear.

stories.headline: Update: Russia Launches Massive Strikes on Ukraine, Killing Civilians in Kyiv and Zelensky's Hometown
stories.summary:
Russia fired more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles at Ukraine, including 27 ballistic missiles, some with cluster warheads, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky. Overnight strikes killed at least eight civilians and wounded more than two dozen. At least seven people were killed in Kyiv and 17 injured in the same assault.

In Kryvyi Rih, Zelensky's hometown, a ballistic missile attack killed at least two people, including a seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old paramedic. Rescue workers were hit when they arrived at the scene, a tactic known as a double-tap strike. Forty-two people were injured, including four children, and 27 were hospitalized in serious condition, said Oleksandr Vilkul, head of the Kryvyi Rih Defence Council.

The attack fit a pattern of heavy Russian retaliation for high-profile Ukrainian strikes, such as those this week on the Kerch Bridge. It also added to uncertainty about U.S.-brokered peace talks. President Trump said the talks were "stuck in the mud like Putin's tanks," adding, "You got two guys who don't know how to end it, we're trying to help them." Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on possible terms.

Separately, European leaders condemned the Russian missile that landed in Poland. The UK's defense intelligence chief said he was confident Russia does not actively seek war with NATO.

stories.headline: Update: Wall Street Tumbles as AI Worries Push S&P 500 Into Correction
stories.summary:
U.S. stocks fell sharply to end the week as concerns about the artificial intelligence sector rattled investors. All three major averages closed deeply in the red. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell more than 900 points, and the Nasdaq dropped more than 5 percent, erasing all of its gains for the year.

The S&P 500 is now down more than 10 percent from its recent high, which puts it in what investors call correction territory. Investors are weighing the health of the AI sector after the leadership upheaval at Nvidia and the record initial public offering of Anthropic, which priced at $83 a share and valued the company above $1 trillion.

The selloff deepens a decline that began earlier in the week, when Anthropic shares fell back toward their IPO price. The AI industry has driven much of the market's gains in recent years, so doubts about its prospects carry wide implications for retirement accounts and the broader economy. Analysts will watch whether the slide continues when trading resumes Monday.

stories.headline: COP31 Climate Talks Deadlocked Over Fossil Fuel Language
stories.summary:
Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey ran through the night and remain deadlocked, with countries unable to agree on a new global climate deal. A group led by France and Panama pushed back against a draft that made no reference to reducing demand for fossil fuels. A new and potentially final text is expected Saturday.

Island states, Panama and EU nations including Spain, France, Belgium, Sweden and Finland want a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal restored after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal. Panama's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said a decision that does not mention fossil fuels is "not acceptable." France's Monique Barbut criticized references to carbon capture as a license to keep burning oil and gas. Separately, the Africa Group is fighting for more adaptation funding, saying it did not come to the talks "to beg."

Australia's Chris Bowen, who is leading the negotiations, argued the summit should focus on implementation and the shift to clean energy. For the first time at a COP, the draft Antalya Accords acknowledge that the goal of limiting warming to 1.5C has been missed and that the world is entering a period of overshoot. Scientists warn that beyond that point millions more people will face sea level rise and extreme heat.
